physics of MIG welding. So you have a
wire that comes out of the end of the
gun here and there's an electrical arc

metal. At the same time, this wire feeds

There are more transfer modes than

think about the physics of MIG welding,

something like a spray transfer here,

feeding wire in and everything is happy.
The issue with that is
it puts too much heat into the material.
And so in order to reduce the amount of
heat, you need to turn that arc on and
off basically. And that's done most
commonly with the short circuit transfer
mode. And that's where you hear that
crackling, frying bacon sound that most
MIG welds have. It's because you're
running a short circuit transfer. So the
wire comes down and creates a short
circuit when it hits the material, then
an arc starts and it burns or melts its
way up the wire until that arc goes out
and it turns off again. And that cycle
repeats over and over again, and that
reduces your heat input so you can weld
on thinner metal, you can weld out of
position like vertical up, and it's
really become the most common for
general fabrication use.
Well, the problem with it or the
challenge with it is you're relying on
physics, much like tuning a carburetor
to have your voltage and wire speed
balance such that it runs just right.

whack a lot of the time, this can, too.
And on top of that, it doesn't really
work well on materials like aluminum.
That's where pulse welding comes in, and
it's actually a pulsed spray transfer in
most cases, at least what we're talking
about here. And the pulse uses
electronics to increase and decrease
your weld current so that you control

short circuit, which can create spatter

going from a carburetor to fuel
injection with an electronically
controlled process.
